verses.text: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.
We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.
When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal.
Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.
In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things. Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.
The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.
All kinds of animals, birds, reptiles, and creatures of the sea are being tamed and have been tamed by man,
but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God's likeness.
Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be!
Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring?
My brothers, can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.
Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.
But if you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth.
Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice.
But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere.
Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness.

context.author: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (1:1). Tradition identifies him with James the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem.
context.genre: Letter with the feel of wisdom literature and a sermon
context.audience: Probably Jewish Christians living outside the land of Israel (“the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” 1:1). Some take the phrase as a title for all of God's people.
context.setting: James warns that teachers will be judged strictly, and turns to the tongue: small like a bit in a horse’s mouth or a rudder on a ship, but able to set a forest on fire. No one can tame it. He contrasts earthly wisdom, marked by jealousy and selfish ambition, with the wisdom from above.
context.custom: Teachers were highly honored, so many wanted the role. A bit and a ship's steering oar were everyday tools, and fire in dry woodland could spread fast. The phrase in v.6 that some Bibles render “the course of his life” is literally a wheel of birth or origin (trochos tes geneseos). Scholars debate what it means, and it probably refers to the cycle or course of life.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 4 explains where quarrels come from.
context.timelineBible: Compare Proverbs 18:21 (death and life are in the power of the tongue), and Psalm 12:3-4, 34:13 and 140:3 on lips and tongues. James 3:9 recalls Genesis 1:26-27, where people are made in God's likeness. The wisdom from above is peace-loving (v.17); Proverbs 3:17 says all of wisdom's paths are peace.
context.sparkNotes: Not many should become teachers, since they will be judged more strictly. We all stumble. The tongue is a small member but boasts great things. It is a fire, a world of unrighteousness, a restless evil. With it we bless the Lord and curse people made in his likeness. Who is wise and understanding among you? Show it by good conduct. Earthly wisdom is jealous and selfish. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits.

translation.meaning: To lead with a bit, to control.
Peace-loving. Wisdom from above makes for peace.

otBackground.note: They sharpen their tongues like a serpent; the poison of vipers is on their lips (compare James 3:8).
Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
People are made in God's likeness (James 3:9).

overview.summary: The tongue is small but powerful and hard to tame. True wisdom shows itself in gentle, merciful living rather than jealousy and selfish ambition.

history.t: Teaching was honored work in the early church (1 Corinthians 12:28; Acts 13:1). James warns that those who teach will be judged more strictly (3:1), and he ties the warning to the tongue.

The word "hell" in 3:6 is Gehenna, from the Hebrew name of the Hinnom Valley just south of Jerusalem. In the Old Testament the valley was linked with child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32), and later Jewish writers used its name for the place of final punishment. Outside this verse, the New Testament uses Gehenna only in Matthew, Mark and Luke.

customs.t: A horse was steered by a bit in its mouth, and a ship by a steering oar at the stern. James uses both as pictures of a small part that directs a large body (3:3-4).
James asks whether a fig tree can grow olives, a grapevine figs, or a salt spring produce fresh water (3:12). Jesus also used trees and their fruit to show what a person is like (Matthew 7:16-20).

archaeology.t: The back of the Princeton leaf of Papyrus 20 has James 3:3-9, the passage about the bit, the rudder and the tongue that no one can tame.

Bronze and iron horse bits survive from many ancient sites, including a Greek bit of the 4th or 3rd century BC in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. A steering oar from a 1st-century Roman river boat, found in Germany, is in Cologne. Seagoing ships were steered by oars of this kind at the stern.

overview.discussion: James says the tongue can bless God and curse people. How do my words move between blessing and cursing in the same day?
